# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**ARIES physiological logging.** ARIES (Mohan et al., 1992) logs changes *physiologically*: physical addressing to a page, logical description of the change within the page. Every log record carries a monotonically increasing **Log Sequence Number (LSN)**; every page stores a **pageLSN** recording the last update applied to it. Two invariants govern durability: the **WAL protocol** (a page may not be flushed to disk before the log record describing its change is flushed — enforced by comparing pageLSN to flushedLSN) and **force-log-at-commit** (all of a transaction's log records, including the commit record, must reach stable storage before commit is acknowledged). Log records are backward-chained per transaction via **prevLSN**, enabling rollback without scanning the whole log.

**Group commit.** Forcing the log on every commit would make commit throughput fsync-bound. Group commit batches the commit records of many concurrent transactions into a single log flush, amortizing one fsync across N transactions at the cost of small added commit latency. PostgreSQL exposes this via `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings`; MySQL/InnoDB implements binary-log group commit with leader/follower flush stages.

**Torn-page protection: full-page writes vs. doublewrite buffer.** Physiological redo requires that a page be internally consistent before a delta is reapplied; a crash mid-way through an 8–16 KB page write (a **torn page**) violates this. PostgreSQL uses **full-page writes (FPW)**: the first modification of a page after each checkpoint logs the entire page image, so redo can restore the page wholesale. InnoDB instead uses the **doublewrite buffer**: pages are written first to a contiguous doublewrite area, fsynced, then written in place; recovery repairs torn pages from the doublewrite copy, keeping redo records small.

**Fuzzy checkpointing.** Rather than quiescing the system, a fuzzy checkpoint writes `begin_checkpoint`/`end_checkpoint` records containing the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** and **Transaction Table** snapshots, without forcing dirty pages out. This bounds recovery time (redo starts at the minimum **recLSN** in the DPT) while leaving the buffer pool's write-back policy **steal/no-force** — dirty uncommitted pages may be stolen, and committed pages need not be forced — which is precisely what undo and redo logging make safe.

## 2. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

**PostgreSQL tuple versioning (xmin/xmax + snapshots + VACUUM).** PostgreSQL stores versions in-place in the heap: each tuple carries **xmin** (creating XID) and **xmax** (deleting/updating XID). A statement's **snapshot** (xmin horizon, xmax, in-progress XID list) plus the commit-status bits in **pg_xact (CLOG)** determine visibility. Updates create new tuple versions chained via **ctid**; dead versions are reclaimed by **VACUUM**, which also freezes old XIDs to prevent 32-bit **transaction-ID wraparound**. **HOT (Heap-Only Tuple)** updates avoid index churn when indexed columns are unchanged.

**InnoDB undo-log versioning with read views.** InnoDB updates rows in place and writes the before-image to **undo logs** in the rollback segment; each row carries hidden **DB_TRX_ID** and **DB_ROLL_PTR** columns. A reader with an older **read view** walks the roll-pointer chain, reconstructing the visible version. The **purge** thread garbage-collects undo records no longer visible to any read view. This is "newest-in-place, old-versions-elsewhere," the dual of PostgreSQL's design.

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain snapshot isolation admits **write skew** and read-only anomalies. SSI (Cahill et al. 2008; Ports & Grittner's PostgreSQL implementation) tracks **rw-antidependencies** using non-blocking **SIREAD locks** and aborts a transaction when it detects the **dangerous structure**: two consecutive rw-antidependency edges (T1 →rw T2 →rw T3) with the pivot's neighbors committing in a conflicting order — a provably necessary condition for any SI serialization anomaly.

**Hekaton timestamp-ordered MVCC.** Microsoft's Hekaton (SQL Server in-memory OLTP) gives each version a `[begin, end)` timestamp validity interval, uses entirely **lock-free (latch-free) Bw-tree/hash indexes** over versions, performs optimistic **validation** of read sets and scan predicates at commit, and resolves commit dependencies without blocking readers — demonstrating MVCC fully decoupled from latching.

## 3. LSM Trees

**Memtable → SSTable flush pipeline.** A Log-Structured Merge tree (O'Neil et al., 1996) absorbs writes into an in-memory **memtable** (typically a skiplist), made durable by its own WAL. When full, the memtable becomes immutable and is flushed as a sorted, immutable **SSTable** (Sorted String Table) with a sparse index and per-block metadata. All writes are sequential I/O; deletes are logical **tombstones** that mask older versions until compaction purges them past gc_grace (Cassandra's `gc_grace_seconds` guards against tombstone loss and deleted-data resurrection).

**Compaction strategies: leveled vs. size-tiered.** **Leveled compaction** (RocksDB/LevelDB) organizes levels L1…Ln with exponentially growing capacity and non-overlapping key ranges within a level; compaction merges one SSTable into the overlapping files of the next level. It minimizes **space amplification** (~1.1×) and read amplification but pays high **write amplification** (~10× per level). **Size-tiered compaction (STCS)** (Cassandra default, RocksDB "universal") merges SSTables of similar size into bigger ones: low write amplification, but overlapping ranges inflate read and space amplification. The RUM conjecture and the **Monkey** work (Dayan et al.) formalize this read/write/space-amplification tradeoff and optimize Bloom-filter bit allocation per level.

**Bloom filters and fence pointers.** Each SSTable carries a **Bloom filter** so point lookups skip tables that provably lack the key (false positives possible, false negatives impossible — tunable via bits/key), and **fence pointers** (block index entries) so at most one block per consulted SSTable is read. Range scans cannot use Bloom filters, which is why prefix Bloom filters and leveled layouts matter for scan-heavy workloads.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Structure modification operations: splits, merges, redistribution.** An insert into a full leaf triggers a **node split**: half the keys move to a new right sibling and a **separator key** is posted to the parent, possibly cascading to a root split (the only way a B+tree grows in height). Underflow on delete triggers **redistribution (key rotation)** from a sibling or a **merge/coalesce** with separator demotion. Practical engines (InnoDB, PostgreSQL nbtree) often defer merges, tolerating underfull nodes and reclaiming empty pages lazily.

**Lehman–Yao B-link trees.** The B-link tree adds to every node a **right-sibling pointer** and a **high key**. A reader that lands on a node whose high key is less than its search key simply "moves right," chasing the sibling pointer — so a concurrent split need not lock the parent and child atomically. This permits safe traversal with only one latch held at a time and no read latches on interior nodes in some variants; PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Lehman–Yao implementation.

**Latch coupling (crabbing) and optimistic descent.** Classical concurrent descent uses **latch coupling**: latch child, verify it is "safe" (won't split/merge under the pending operation), release parent. **Optimistic lock coupling** and OLFIT-style schemes replace read latches with version counters validated after the read, drastically reducing coherence traffic on modern multicores.

**Recovery-safe SMOs and phantom prevention: ARIES/IM and next-key locking.** ARIES/IM executes a split/merge as a **nested top action** terminated by a dummy CLR, so a completed SMO survives even if the enclosing transaction rolls back, and in-flight SMOs are undone atomically. Logical key deletion plus **key-range / next-key locking** (ARIES/KVL; InnoDB's next-key locks = record lock + gap lock on the following interval) prevents **phantoms** under serializable isolation by locking the gap into which a phantom would be inserted.

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**The basic protocol and its force-writes.** Phase 1: the coordinator sends PREPARE; each participant force-writes a **prepare record** (entering the **in-doubt/prepared** state, retaining all locks) and votes YES/NO. Phase 2: upon unanimous YES the coordinator force-writes a **commit record** (the protocol's single commit point), then broadcasts COMMIT; participants force-write their decision and ACK, after which the coordinator writes an **end record** and forgets the transaction. A prepared participant may not unilaterally decide — this is the **blocking problem**: if the coordinator fails, in-doubt participants hold locks until it recovers (the **cooperative termination protocol** lets participants query each other, resolving some but not all cases).

**Presumed abort / presumed commit.** **Presumed abort (PA)** — the industry standard (R*, XA implementations) — lets the coordinator answer "abort" to any inquiry about an unknown transaction, so abort records need not be forced and no ACKs are needed on abort; it also enables the **read-only optimization** (a read-only participant votes READ-ONLY and skips phase 2). **Presumed commit (PC)** inverts the presumption, saving messages on the common commit path but requiring the coordinator to force-log participant lists *before* prepare to remain safe.

**Non-blocking alternatives: 3PC and Paxos Commit.** **Three-phase commit** (Skeen) inserts a pre-commit state so no state is adjacent to both commit and abort, achieving non-blocking termination under a synchronous, no-partition model — assumptions too fragile for practice. **Paxos Commit** (Gray & Lamport, 2006) runs one Paxos consensus instance per participant's vote with 2F+1 acceptors, making the commit decision itself fault-tolerant; classic 2PC is exactly Paxos Commit with F = 0. Modern systems embody this pattern: Spanner runs 2PC with each participant and the coordinator being a Paxos group. The **XA** specification standardizes the transaction-manager/resource-manager interface (xa_prepare, xa_commit, xa_recover) for heterogeneous 2PC.

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport scalar clocks.** Lamport (1978) defines the **happened-before** partial order (→): program order, send-before-receive, and transitivity. Each process keeps a counter, incremented per event; messages carry timestamps and receivers set C := max(C, ts) + 1. This guarantees **clock consistency**: e → f ⇒ C(e) < C(f), but not the converse — concurrent events may have ordered timestamps, so Lamport clocks can impose a total order (with PID tiebreak) but cannot *detect* concurrency.

**Vector clocks and (dotted) version vectors.** A vector clock holds one counter per process; VC(e) < VC(f) **iff** e → f, so incomparable vectors certify concurrency (Fidge/Mattern). **Version vectors** apply this per data item for replica divergence detection (Dynamo's sibling detection on conflicting puts). **Dotted version vectors (DVVs)**, used in Riak, add a "dot" identifying the exact event of the latest write, correctly handling multiple clients writing through the same server and bounding sibling explosion where naive client-ID version vectors fail or grow unboundedly.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** HLC (Kulkarni et al., 2014) combines a physical component (max physical time seen) with a logical counter for causality within the same physical tick. HLC timestamps are close to wall-clock time (bounded drift from NTP), fit in 64 bits, and preserve e → f ⇒ hlc(e) < hlc(f). CockroachDB uses HLC for MVCC timestamps and causality propagation across sessions. Contrast **Spanner TrueTime**, which is not a logical clock at all: GPS/atomic clocks expose a bounded uncertainty interval [earliest, latest], and **commit-wait** (sleeping out the uncertainty ε before releasing locks) yields **external consistency (strict serializability)** — trading specialized hardware for the causality metadata logical clocks must carry.

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Weighted voting and R+W>N intersection.** Gifford (1979) assigns each replica votes; reads need R votes, writes W votes, with **R + W > N** forcing every read quorum to intersect every write quorum (and **W > N/2** preventing conflicting concurrent writes). This yields read-your-latest-acknowledged-write at the replica-set level, with tunable latency: R=1,W=N for read-heavy, W=1,R=N for write-heavy workloads. Grid, tree, and hierarchical quorums trade availability against quorum size (down to O(√N)).

**Dynamo-style sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, read repair.** Dynamo (and Cassandra/Riak) relax strict membership: a **sloppy quorum** accepts writes on the first N *healthy* nodes along the consistent-hashing ring, with **hinted handoff** — a stand-in node stores the write plus a hint and forwards it when the home replica recovers. This maximizes write availability but forfeits strict quorum intersection (even R+W>N can miss the latest write during handoff). Convergence is driven by **read repair** (reconciling stale replicas detected during reads via version vectors) and **anti-entropy** using **Merkle trees** to cheaply diff replica key ranges.

**Consensus majority quorums and Flexible Paxos.** Paxos and Raft use majority quorums so any two quorums intersect, ensuring a new leader's quorum contains at least one node that saw every committed entry (Raft additionally requires the up-to-date-log election restriction). **Flexible Paxos** (Howard et al., 2016) proves that only phase-1 (leader-election) quorums and phase-2 (replication) quorums need intersect — not two phase-2 quorums — so one can commit with, e.g., Q2 = 2 of 5 if Q1 = 4 of 5, shrinking the steady-state write quorum at the cost of more expensive leader changes. **Witness replicas** (vote-only, log-light members) are a practical quorum-cost optimization in Spanner and others.

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery: Analysis, Redo, Undo.** (i) **Analysis** scans forward from the last checkpoint, reconstructing the **Transaction Table** (loser transactions and their lastLSNs) and **Dirty Page Table** (page → recLSN). (ii) **Redo** starts at min(recLSN) and **repeats history**: it reapplies *every* update — including those of losers — whenever pageLSN < record LSN, restoring the exact pre-crash state. Repeating history is the keystone that makes fine-grained (record-level) locking and physiological logging recoverable. (iii) **Undo** rolls back losers in reverse LSN order, writing a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)** for each undone update. CLRs are **redo-only** and carry an **undoNextLSN** pointer skipping already-compensated work, guaranteeing that recovery is **idempotent** and that repeated crashes during recovery never undo the same action twice or extend the log unboundedly.

**Fuzzy checkpoints bounding recovery.** Because ARIES checkpoints log the DPT and transaction table rather than flushing pages, the redo scan start and analysis scan length are bounded by background-writer progress — recovery time is tuned by checkpoint frequency without ever stalling normal processing (contrast sharp/quiescent checkpoints).

**Shadow paging (the contrasting design).** System R's recovery (Lorie) maintained a **shadow page table**: updates go to fresh pages, and commit atomically swings the root pointer from the shadow to the current page table — no redo/undo of data pages needed. Costs: destroyed physical clustering, expensive garbage collection, and page-granularity commits that conflict with fine-grained concurrency — the reasons ARIES-style WAL won. The idea survives in **copy-on-write B-trees** (LMDB, where a crash simply abandons unreachable pages) and ZFS/Btrfs.

**Torn-page and media recovery.** Redo correctness presumes readable, un-torn pages: PostgreSQL's **full-page writes** restore the first post-checkpoint image during redo; InnoDB's **doublewrite buffer** repairs torn pages before redo begins; page checksums detect corruption. **Media recovery** restores a backup and replays archived log (PostgreSQL continuous archiving / point-in-time recovery), the same redo machinery driving physical **streaming replication** — crash recovery, PITR, and replication are one mechanism at different scopes.

---

**Synthesis.** The through-line is a small set of invariants — log-before-data, repeating history, quorum intersection, happened-before preservation, and single-point atomic decision — instantiated by different named mechanisms per layer: ARIES/CLRs/fuzzy checkpoints for durability; snapshots, undo chains, and SSI for isolation; LSM compaction and B-link SMOs for index maintenance; presumed-abort 2PC hardened by Paxos Commit for atomic distribution; and Lamport/vector/HLC clocks plus (flexible) quorums for ordering and availability.

Answer: The brief above covers all eight areas in depth with 3+ precisely named mechanisms each — WAL (ARIES physiological logging with LSN/pageLSN and force-log-at-commit, group commit, full-page writes vs. InnoDB doublewrite, fuzzy checkpoints); MVCC (PostgreSQL xmin/xmax+VACUUM, InnoDB undo logs/read views/purge, SSI with SIREAD locks, Hekaton); LSM trees (memtable/SSTable flush, leveled vs. size-tiered compaction, Bloom filters/fence pointers/tombstones); B+tree maintenance (splits/merges/redistribution, Lehman–Yao B-link trees, latch coupling, ARIES/IM nested top actions and next-key locking); 2PC (presumed abort/presumed commit, blocking problem and 3PC, Paxos Commit, XA); logical clocks (Lamport, vector/dotted version vectors, HLC vs. TrueTime); quorums (Gifford weighted voting R+W>N, Dynamo sloppy quorums/hinted handoff/read repair, Raft majorities and Flexible Paxos); and crash recovery (ARIES analysis/redo/undo with repeating history and CLRs, fuzzy checkpoints, shadow paging, torn-page/media recovery).

response.content:
# Distributed Transaction and Recovery Internals

A deep technical treatment of atomic commitment, logical time, quorum-based replication, and crash recovery.

---

## 1. Two-Phase Commit (2PC) and Atomic Commitment

### 1.1 The basic protocol

2PC solves **atomic commitment**: all participants in a distributed transaction must reach the same decision (commit or abort), and a commit decision requires unanimous yes-votes.

**Phase 1 — Prepare (voting phase):**
1. The **coordinator** force-writes a *begin-commit* (or relies on the prepare request itself) and sends `PREPARE` to all participants.
2. Each participant that can commit **force-writes a prepare log record** (containing all redo/undo information and lock state needed to survive a crash) to stable storage *before* replying `VOTE-YES`. From this moment the participant is **in doubt** (uncertain): it has surrendered the unilateral right to abort and must hold its locks.
3. A participant that cannot commit replies `VOTE-NO` and may abort immediately (a no-vote is a veto; no stable record is strictly required because of presumed abort, below).

**Phase 2 — Commit/abort (decision phase):**
1. On receiving yes-votes from all participants, the coordinator **force-writes a commit record** — this write is the *commit point*; the transaction's fate is now decided regardless of subsequent failures.
2. The coordinator sends `COMMIT` (or `ABORT`) to all participants.
3. Each participant force-writes its local commit/abort record, releases locks, and replies `ACK`.
4. When all ACKs arrive, the coordinator writes a (non-forced) *end* record and can forget the transaction (garbage-collect its protocol state).

Message/log cost for the unoptimized protocol with N participants: roughly 2N forced coordinator-side + participant-side log writes and ~4N messages per transaction. The optimizations below exist to shave forced writes and messages.

### 1.2 Presumed Abort (PA)

Observation: if the coordinator finds **no information** about a transaction in its protocol state after a crash, a recovering participant's inquiry can safely be answered "abort" — provided the coordinator never commits without a forced record. Thus:

- The coordinator need **not force-write abort records** and need not log anything before the prepare phase; aborts leave no durable trace ("presumption of abort").
- Participants need not ACK abort messages, and the coordinator need not remember aborted transactions.
- **Read-only participants** reply `VOTE-READ-ONLY` and drop out entirely: they write no log records and receive no second-phase message. For a fully read-only transaction, 2PC degenerates to one round with zero forced writes — the single most important practical optimization.

PA is the variant mandated by most industrial systems (it underlies the behavior assumed by **XA**, and is the default in R*, where it was first described by Mohan, Lindsay & Obermarck).

### 1.3 Presumed Commit (PC)

The dual optimization: missing information means "commit," so participants need not ACK commit decisions and the coordinator need not force the commit record's *end*. But a naive PC is unsafe: if the coordinator crashes between sending PREPARE and deciding, recovering participants would wrongly presume commit. The fix: the coordinator must **force-write a collecting/initiation record naming all participants *before* sending PREPARE**. Consequently:

- PC saves one forced log write and one message *per participant* in the common commit case (no commit ACKs, no forced participant commit records in some variants).
- PC costs one extra forced coordinator write per transaction (the initiation record) and makes aborts more expensive.
- Because commits dominate aborts, PC can win on update-heavy workloads; PA wins when read-only subtransactions are common. **New Presumed Commit** (Lampson & Lomet, 1993) removes the extra forced initiation write by logging participant sets lazily and tracking a stable low-water mark of potentially-initiated transaction IDs.

### 1.4 The blocking problem

2PC is a **blocking protocol**: a participant that has voted yes and then loses contact with the coordinator (coordinator crash, partition) is stuck in the in-doubt window. It cannot abort (the coordinator may have committed) and cannot commit (another participant may have voted no). It must **hold all its locks** — including write locks on hot data — until the coordinator recovers or a termination protocol resolves it. The *cooperative termination protocol* (ask other participants) helps only if some participant already knows the outcome; if all operational participants are in doubt, they block. Skeen's result formalizes this: **no atomic commitment protocol can be non-blocking in the presence of communication failures/partitions**, and 2PC blocks even under the weaker crash-stop model because of its single point of decision.

### 1.5 Three-Phase Commit (3PC)

Skeen's 3PC inserts a **pre-commit** phase between prepare and commit: the coordinator disseminates "everyone voted yes" (`PRE-COMMIT`) and collects acknowledgments before sending `COMMIT`. This enforces the **non-blocking property's structural requirement**: no participant commits while another can still be in a state from which abort is reachable, and vice versa — there is no state adjacent to both commit and abort. Under a **synchronous system with crash-stop failures and no partitions**, surviving participants can run an election and a termination protocol that safely completes the transaction, so 3PC is non-blocking there. In practice 3PC is almost never deployed because:

- It adds a full round-trip and forced write in the common case.
- Under **network partitions** it is unsafe (two sides can elect coordinators and decide differently) unless combined with quorums (Keidar & Dolev's E3PC), at which point one has effectively reinvented consensus.

### 1.6 Paxos Commit (Gray & Lamport, 2006)

"Consensus on Transaction Commit" reframes atomic commitment correctly: run **one independent Paxos consensus instance per participant's vote** (prepared/aborted), with the transaction committing iff every instance chooses "prepared." Key points:

- Each participant acts as the *leader-proposed value source* for its own instance; a set of 2F+1 acceptors replicates each vote. The 2PC coordinator is replaced by the Paxos leader, which is **no longer a single point of failure** — any F failures are tolerated without blocking.
- 2PC is exactly the **F = 0 degenerate case** of Paxos Commit (one acceptor = the coordinator), making precise the folklore that "2PC is consensus with one acceptor."
- Latency in the failure-free case equals 2PC's (using the Phase-2a/2b fast path with pre-prepared ballot 0), at the cost of more messages (each participant's vote goes to 2F+1 acceptors).
- If a participant is slow, the leader can propose "aborted" on its behalf in a higher ballot; Paxos's quorum intersection prevents conflicting decisions.

Modern systems (Spanner's 2PC-over-Paxos-groups, CockroachDB's parallel commits over Raft ranges) are architectural descendants: layer 2PC *across* replicated state machines so each "participant" is itself highly available.

### 1.7 XA

**X/Open XA** is the standardized C interface between a **transaction manager (TM)** and **resource managers (RMs)** in the DTP model: `xa_start`/`xa_end` (associate a branch, identified by an XID, with an RM), `xa_prepare`, `xa_commit`, `xa_rollback`, `xa_recover` (enumerate in-doubt branches after a crash), plus `xa_commit` with `TMONEPHASE` for the **one-phase-commit optimization** when there is a single RM. XA assumes presumed abort. Its chronic operational pathology is the **heuristic outcome**: an operator or RM unilaterally resolves an in-doubt branch (`XA_HEURCOM`/`XA_HEURRB`/`XA_HEURMIX`) to break blocking, sacrificing atomicity — a direct consequence of §1.4.

## 2. Logical Clocks

### 2.1 Lamport scalar clocks and happened-before

Lamport (1978) defines the **happened-before** relation `→` as the smallest transitive relation such that (a) if a and b are events on the same process and a precedes b, then a → b; (b) if a is the send of a message and b its receipt, a → b. Events unordered by → are **concurrent** (a ∥ b). → is an irreflexive partial order — it is *potential causality*.

A **Lamport clock** assigns each event a scalar `C(e)`:
- Local event / send: `C := C + 1`.
- Receive of message carrying timestamp `t`: `C := max(C, t) + 1`.

This guarantees the **clock condition**: `a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b)`. The converse fails — `C(a) < C(b)` does **not** imply causality — so Lamport clocks cannot *detect* concurrency. Breaking ties by process ID yields a total order consistent with causality, which Lamport used to build a totally-ordered multicast / distributed mutual exclusion algorithm; the same construction underlies timestamp ordering in many systems.

### 2.2 Vector clocks and version vectors

**Vector clocks** (Fidge 1988, Mattern 1989) carry an N-entry vector `V`, one slot per process:
- Local/send at process i: `V[i] += 1`.
- Receive with vector `W`: `V := pointwise-max(V, W); V[i] += 1`.

They **characterize** causality exactly: `a → b ⇔ V(a) < V(b)` (pointwise ≤ with at least one strict), and `a ∥ b ⇔ V(a) ∦ V(b)` (incomparable). Charron-Bost proved N entries are necessary in the worst case to capture causality among N processes.

**Version vectors** (Parker et al., 1983, for LOCUS) are the data-centric sibling: one vector *per replicated object*, incremented by the replica performing an update, used to detect **conflicting (concurrent) versions** during anti-entropy — the mechanism Dynamo popularized for sibling detection.

**Dotted version vectors (DVVs)** — used in **Riak** — fix a correctness/efficiency flaw in server-side version vectors under the get/put pattern: when a client writes with a stale causal *context* and the server merely increments its own counter, concurrent writes through the same server can be falsely ordered (silent sibling overwrite) or siblings explode. A DVV represents a version as a contiguous vector-clock prefix **plus one discrete "dot"** `(server_id, counter)` identifying the exact event that created that version. The dot lets the server mark the new write as causally dominating exactly the client-supplied context while remaining **concurrent** with other versions not covered by it. This bounds metadata by the number of replica nodes (not clients) and yields precise sibling semantics.

### 2.3 Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)

HLC (Kulkarni, Demirbas et al., 2014) fuses physical and logical time into a timestamp `(l, c)`:
- `l` tracks the maximum physical clock value (`pt`) seen so far: `l := max(l, pt, l_msg)`.
- `c` is a logical counter used only to break ties when `l` doesn't advance: reset to 0 when `l` jumps, incremented otherwise.

Properties: (1) the **logical clock condition** `e → f ⇒ hlc(e) < hlc(f)` holds, enabling causality tracking; (2) `l` stays within the physical clock's uncertainty bound of real time (`|l − pt| ≤ ε` under maximum clock skew ε), so HLC timestamps are *meaningful as wall-clock time*; (3) fixed size, no per-node vector.

**CockroachDB** uses HLC for MVCC timestamps and transaction ordering: a node receiving a message with a higher HLC ratchets its clock forward, guaranteeing that causally-related transactions get monotone timestamps. Because CockroachDB only *bounds* skew (configured `max-offset`, default 500 ms) rather than measuring it precisely, a read encountering a value in its **uncertainty interval** `(ts, ts + max_offset]` must perform an *uncertainty restart* at a higher timestamp — it cannot know whether that write really preceded it.

### 2.4 Contrast: Spanner TrueTime

**TrueTime** (Spanner, 2012) is not a logical clock at all: it exposes bounded-uncertainty *physical* time via GPS + atomic-clock time masters — `TT.now()` returns an interval `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain absolute time, with ε typically 1–7 ms. Spanner achieves **external consistency** (linearizable commit order = timestamp order) via **commit wait**: a transaction with commit timestamp `s` delays releasing its effects until `TT.after(s)` is true, i.e., waits out the uncertainty ε. The contrast:

| | HLC (CockroachDB) | TrueTime (Spanner) |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware | commodity NTP | GPS/atomic clock infrastructure |
| Causality | tracked logically, free | purchased by waiting |
| Cost of uncertainty | reader-side (uncertainty restarts) | writer-side (commit-wait latency ≈ ε) |
| Guarantee | causal/serializable; no global linearizability of non-communicating txns | external consistency (strict serializability) |

HLC gets causality "for free" through message piggybacking but cannot order causally-independent transactions in real-time order; TrueTime pays latency to make timestamp order coincide with real-time order even for transactions that never communicate.

## 3. Quorum Systems

### 3.1 Gifford weighted voting (1979)

Each of N replicas is assigned a **vote weight**; reads must assemble a **read quorum** of weight ≥ R, writes a **write quorum** of weight ≥ W, subject to:

- **R + W > V** (total votes): every read quorum intersects every write quorum, so a read always sees at least one copy of the latest completed write (identified by a **version number** per replica; the read returns the highest-versioned copy).
- **W > V/2**: any two write quorums intersect, serializing writes and preventing split-brain version divergence.

Tuning: `R=1, W=V` (read-one/write-all) optimizes reads; `W=1` is disallowed by the second constraint in the strict scheme. Weighted votes let an operator bias availability toward well-connected or reliable replicas, and **weak representatives** (zero-vote caches) serve reads without participating in quorums. Gifford's scheme is the ancestor of all R/W quorum replication.

### 3.2 Strict quorums: R + W > N in modern stores

Leaderless stores (Cassandra, Riak, Voldemort) expose per-operation R and W over N replicas. **R + W > N** gives read-your-latest-write *intersection*, but note the caveats: without a concurrency-control layer, intersection alone does not give linearizability (partial writes, read-write races require read repair with write-back, i.e., ABD-style algorithms); and version numbers must be replaced by vector clocks or last-write-wins timestamps to order concurrent client writes.

### 3.3 Dynamo: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, read repair

Amazon's Dynamo deliberately **relaxes strict intersection** for availability:

- **Sloppy quorum**: writes go to the first N *healthy* nodes on the consistent-hashing **preference list**, skipping failed ones. W acknowledgments from these — possibly including nodes outside the canonical home set — complete the write. Consequence: read and write quorums are **not guaranteed to intersect** during failures; the system is eventually consistent by design ("always writeable" for the shopping cart).
- **Hinted handoff**: a stand-in node stores the write with a **hint** naming the intended home replica; it delivers the data when the home node recovers, then deletes its local copy. This restores full replication after transient failures without blocking writes.
- **Read repair**: a coordinator performing a read that observes stale replicas (detected via version-vector comparison) pushes the up-to-date version back to them — convergence piggybacked on the read path.
- Backstop: **anti-entropy with Merkle trees** synchronizes key ranges between replicas to catch what read repair misses, and **vector clocks with client-side reconciliation** (or application merge, e.g., cart union) resolve siblings from sloppy-quorum divergence.

### 3.4 Majority quorums in Paxos and Raft

Consensus protocols use **majority quorums** (⌈(N+1)/2⌉ of N): any two majorities intersect in at least one node. This single intersection property is what makes Paxos safe — a value chosen in ballot b is seen by the Phase-1 quorum of any higher ballot, forcing the new leader to re-propose it — and what makes Raft safe: a candidate must win votes from a majority, which necessarily includes a node holding every committed entry (combined with Raft's **election restriction**: voters refuse candidates whose log is less up-to-date, compared by last term then length). An entry is **committed** once replicated on a majority *in the leader's current term* (Raft §5.4.2's subtlety: entries from prior terms are committed only indirectly). Majority quorums tolerate F failures with N = 2F+1 and, unlike 2PC, never block as long as a majority is live and connected.

### 3.5 Flexible Paxos (Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman, 2016)

FPaxos's insight: Paxos does **not** need all-pairs quorum intersection. The only required intersection is **between Phase-1 (leader election) quorums Q1 and Phase-2 (replication) quorums Q2**: every Q1 must intersect every Q2, i.e., |Q1| + |Q2| > N for simple counting quorums. Two Q2s need not intersect each other, nor two Q1s. Consequences:

- Shrink the steady-state replication quorum: with N = 10, choose |Q2| = 3, |Q1| = 8 — commits touch only 3 nodes (lower latency, less load), at the price of needing 8 for the rare leader election (worse election-time availability).
- **Grid quorums**: Q2 = one row, Q1 = one column of an r×c grid — Q1 ∩ Q2 guaranteed by geometry with quorum sizes O(√N).
- The same relaxation applies to Raft (leader election quorum vs. commit quorum) and explains/justifies deployments like "require all replicas in-sync for writes, any single survivor can lead."

## 4. Crash Recovery

### 4.1 ARIES (Mohan et al., 1992)

ARIES assumes **write-ahead logging (WAL)**: (i) a page's log records are forced to stable storage before the dirty page is written out (undo rule), and (ii) all of a transaction's log records are forced before commit (redo/durability rule). It supports **STEAL** (dirty uncommitted pages may be flushed) and **NO-FORCE** (commit doesn't flush data pages) buffer policies — the high-performance combination that makes both redo and undo necessary. Every page carries a **pageLSN** (LSN of the last log record applied to it), and every log record carries **prevLSN** linking a transaction's records into a backward chain.

**Fuzzy checkpoints** write, without quiescing activity, a `begin_checkpoint`/`end_checkpoint` pair containing snapshots of the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** — mapping each dirty page to its **recLSN** (the LSN of the first record that may have dirtied it since it was last clean) — and the **Transaction Table (TT)** — each active transaction's state and **lastLSN**. No pages are flushed at checkpoint time.

**Restart proceeds in three passes:**

1. **Analysis** — scan forward from the last checkpoint's `begin_checkpoint`, reconstructing the DPT and TT: add transactions on their first record, remove on end records, add pages to the DPT (recLSN = current LSN) when an update record references a page not already present. Output: the set of **loser transactions** (in TT without end record) and the **redoLSN** = min(recLSN over DPT), the earliest point where redo must start.

2. **Redo — "repeating history."** ARIES's signature principle: redo scans forward from redoLSN and reapplies **every** update — including those of loser transactions — restoring the database to its exact state at crash time. A record for page P is skipped only if (a) P ∉ DPT, (b) P's recLSN > record's LSN, or (c) `pageLSN(P) ≥ LSN` (the update already reached disk) — the pageLSN check being the fundamental **idempotence** mechanism. Repeating history is what makes fine-granularity (record-level) locking and logical undo sound: undo always starts from a well-defined, fully-replayed state.

3. **Undo** — roll back losers by following prevLSN chains backward, always undoing the record with the maximum LSN among all losers (a single backward sweep). Each undo action writes a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)**, which is **redo-only** (never undone) and carries **undoNextLSN** = the prevLSN of the record just compensated. After a crash *during* undo, recovery resumes at the undoNextLSN of the last CLR, skipping already-compensated records. This guarantees **bounded undo work** — each update is undone at most once, no matter how many times the system crashes during recovery — and avoids the exponential compensation-of-compensation problem of earlier schemes. CLRs also implement partial rollback to **savepoints** and support logical undo (e.g., B-tree key delete undone by re-insert into a *different* page than the original).

### 4.2 Shadow paging (System R) as contrast

System R's recovery used **shadow paging**: a page table maps logical to physical pages; an update writes a *new* physical page and updates a shadow copy of the page map; commit atomically swings the root pointer from the current map to the new one. Properties, versus ARIES:

- No redo needed for committed data (the atomic pointer swing is the commit), and undo is "discard the new map" — conceptually elegant, NO-STEAL/FORCE-like at the map level.
- Costs that killed it: destroyed **physical clustering** (pages migrate on every update), page-map maintenance and garbage collection overhead, extra I/O for map pages, commit-time map flushing, and — critically — **page-level granularity**: shadow paging alone cannot support record-level locking with concurrent transactions on one page, which is precisely what ARIES's repeating-history + CLR design enables. System R in fact still needed a log *on top of* shadows for transaction undo/redo. Mohan's ARIES paper uses System R as the explicit foil. (Modern echoes: LMDB's copy-on-write B-tree and ZFS/btrfs CoW are shadow-paging descendants, viable where single-writer or page-level semantics suffice.)

### 4.3 Torn-page handling

A crash mid-way through a multi-sector page write leaves a **torn page** (fractured write): some sectors new, some old — a state WAL redo cannot repair if the log holds only *physiological* (byte-diff) records, since neither old nor new page image is intact and the pageLSN itself may be garbage. Mechanisms:

- **PostgreSQL full-page writes (FPW)**: the first modification of a page after each checkpoint logs the **entire page image**; redo restores the full image, making the page's prior torn state irrelevant. Cost: WAL inflation after checkpoints.
- **InnoDB doublewrite buffer**: dirty pages are first written sequentially to a doublewrite area, fsynced, then written to their home locations. On recovery, any torn home page (detected by per-page checksum mismatch) is restored from the doublewrite copy. Trades 2× page-write bandwidth (mostly sequential) for torn-write atomicity.
- **SQL Server torn-page detection / page checksums**: a bit from each 512-byte sector is flipped into the header (or a whole-page checksum computed) so tears are *detected*; repair comes from backup/mirror — detection without inline repair.
- Hardware/filesystem alternatives: atomic-write-capable devices and CoW filesystems (ZFS) make FPW/doublewrite unnecessary (`innodb_doublewrite=OFF` on such stacks).

## 5. How the pieces compose

A modern distributed SQL engine stacks all four areas: each shard is a **Raft/Paxos group** (majority quorums, §3.4) whose leader runs an **ARIES-style or LSM WAL** locally (§4) with torn-write protection; cross-shard transactions run **2PC with presumed abort** where the "coordinator" and each "participant" are replicated groups — Gray–Lamport's resolution of the blocking problem (§1.6); and transaction ordering uses **HLC or TrueTime** timestamps (§2.3–2.4) so that commit timestamps respect causality (or real time) across shards. The historical through-line is consistent: each mechanism (presumed abort, DVVs, flexible quorums, CLRs with undoNextLSN) exists to remove a specific forced write, false conflict, over-strong intersection requirement, or unbounded-recovery pathology from its naive predecessor.
